newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade students turn standoff into street party.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade students turn standoff into street party.

text.p: Determined Serbian students held a street party in front of heavily armed anti-riot cordons as their bid to stare down a police blockade stretched into the night.

In the latest swipe by foreign powers at President Slobodan Milosevic, the United States said his admission of local election defeat in Serbia's second city of Nis was not enough and he could not win world applause by "dribbling out minor concessions".
Thursday marked the 53rd day of protests against the cancellation of municipal poll results by Milosevic's ruling Socialists last November.
Teams of whistle-blowing students played cat and mouse with police cordons in central Belgrade all afternoon.
As soon as one cordon broke up, students would start moving but a fresh police blockade would spring up somewhere else.
By late evening, about 1,500 students were gathered in a side street, watched by police who were changing shift every two hours.

One duo set up a table and chairs in the no man's land between the two groups and calmly played chess as crowds danced to music blaring from the demonstrators' public address system. Supporters brought food and drinks.
The students have vowed they will continue until the police promise not to block the streets to prevent them marching.
"We just hope that the police will come to their senses and finally understand that no measure of repression can stop us," said student leader Cedomir Jovanovic.

One group held up a poster urging police to join their protest. "Be a sport, throw away your truncheon and shield and join your people. You will see that smiles are contagious and very soon you will be allowed to go to your home, sweet home," it said.
Police are enforcing a ban on protest marches imposed after clashes between pro-government and opposition demonstrators on December 24.
The students' action gathered about 3,000 people at its height, while the opposition Zajedno coalition gathered about 20,000 at its daily rally in Republic Square.
On Wednesday, Milosevic admitted Zajedno had won in Nis, but Zajedno leaders vowed protests would continue until all their claims were met.
In Washington, U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the government announcement was "a positive development, but it doesn't go nearly far enough".
"The Serbian government does not have the right to grant the opposition victories that the opposition won on its own in elections," Burns said.
U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum headed for The Hague, Brussels, Sarajevo and Zagreb on Thursday to discuss the crisis in Serbia, deliberately excluding Belgrade.
After a regular meeting in the Dutch capital of U.S. and European Union foreign ministry officials, he will take part in Brussels in a meeting of the five-nation Contact Group on former Yugoslavia.

France said it was sending Paul Poulade, director for continental Europe at the Foreign Ministry, to Belgrade to urge Milosevic to heed an Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) mission's confirmation of the opposition wins.
The government responded to the OSCE report by admitting Zajedno had won in nine wards of Belgrade and three smaller provincial cities.
But it said nothing about Belgrade's policy-making municipal assembly and contended that in the other cities no party won a majority or the results were inconclusive and required further examination.
